utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has decided that the next witness, K79 will give evidence with additional protective measures of voice and image distortion. We've considered carefully the various submissions made by Mr. Ivetic and also by Mr. Ackerman yesterday in relation to the evidence in general. We don't think that we can make a blanket decision at this stage to exclude this evidence. We think that on the face of it, there will be evidence relevant to the indictment. We understand that the witness may be asked about Suva Reka or at least about the forces in the vicinity of Suva Reka, which may be important from the point of view of identification apart from anything else. It would appear that he may give evidence that goes to the question of whether there was an armed conflict and whether the activities were widespread and systematic. He would appear to have evidence to give in relation to Orahovac about which we have heard some evidence already, and it may be that some of what he says has a bearing on the averments in paragraph 95. But it's for counsel to take specific objections if they consider that we are in territory which cannot be said at all to have any relevance to the indictment, and we will consider each individual objection as it is made. We can now hear from the witness, and we need to go into closed session for him to enter the courtroom. Sorry, stop that process. Stop this. I didn't realise this was something else to be dealt with. Let's get back into open session. Utter confusion so often in this place. No sense of organisation. What is the point you now wish to raise, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We had time yesterday to deal with how this witness's evidence would be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since court yesterday, late yesterday afternoon I was given a rough draft translation of a document that we discussed in private session yesterday. In light of that summary, I have reviewed the way the evidence would be -- we would have to present the evidence of the witness. I think it means at that we would have to go into more private session than I originally had foreseen, and I wonder whether it's not going to be sort of so much in and out of private session that it would be better to present the witness's evidence under Rule 92 ter. I did make efforts this morning to notify one of the court officers of this, but I guess the communication hadn't passed, so I apologise. I also should have told also the Registry staff early on. My suggestion is that we simply present the evidence in form of 92 ter. I will have some questions for the witness, but we will only have to go into private session in that regard very few times, and then I think that would just run the whole thing more smoothly. But I'm prepared to do the witness live, and I do understand one of my colleagues on the other side have an objection to this mode of presentation of the evidence. I would note that our witness notification that we filed last week did put the witness down as a live/92 ter witness, although it was actually my intention to present the witness as a live witness, but -- and I don't know, it might also be that the Chamber hasn't had a chance to study the statement sufficiently to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I haven't received the statement, so I don't know what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was requested to send forward a copy of the statement to -- to one of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And that was for legal staff to help with the analysis of whether there might be relevant evidence to be given by this witness, because there isn't enough in the motion. And having been assisted with that, I haven't read the statement in detail to try to familiarise myself with it and have the witness presented to me as a -- well, with part of his evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm perfectly happy going in open session -- in direct examination with the witness, but I just wanted to make the suggestion for the Court to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're all agreed that you should proceed as originally proposed and lead this witness live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you come to the stage where there's something simple that can be presented in writing and you make an appropriate motion, which is the way Rule 92 ter ought to operate, then you can do it. As I said before, there is no such thing as a rule 92 ter witness. You are free to present any part of a witness's evidence in writing if you can justify that as being in the interests of justice. Bearing in mind our experience of the last witness, we doubt if it would be in the interest of justice unless we had had a fair opportunity of reading this in advance if what you intend is to present an extensive statement from the witness. So we think that you should lead him live and only present in writing anything that is clearly relevant and would be in our view clearly evidence which would be in the interests of justice to see in writing rather than here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall now go into closed session for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The noise is caused by blinds behind you rising. I appreciate you can't see them, but we won't start until the noise stops. You will be asked questions by a number of counsel representing both the Prosecution and the six accused persons in this trial, and the first counsel to ask questions will be for the Prosecution, and that is Mr. Marcussen. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, K79.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As the President has just informed you, you have been granted protective measures in order to present -- to protect your identity. There will be times when I will ask that we go into private session. If -- if need be, I would like to ask that you indicate to me if there's an answer you cannot give because you're afraid of revealing the identity and then we'll have to deal with it. Of course, I'll try to avoid this, but I just wanted to ask you to be alert to this yourself as well. Now, first, I would like to show you a piece of paper and ask you if this -- what is written on this paper is a correct reflection of who you are, and I, of course, ask you not to say any names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document has been uploaded. The witness identification sheet has been uploaded into e-court as Exhibit P2641, and I would like to ask that that exhibit be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, would you describe your education for me starting with your primary school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed primary school, a secondary school for agriculture, and a course for policemen. I completed the course for policemen in 1992 in Zemun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And have you done your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1987, in Tuzla, as a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you -- you completed a course as a policeman in 1992. Did you join the police at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Marcussen, the period of military service must be 1997. It's recorded as 1987 on the transcript. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, what year did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before -- before you became a policeman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, so what -- what part of the police did you work in in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in that capacity what -- what kind of work would you do. Just give a brief description.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on the beat. I did patrols, normal police work as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At that point in time, did you have any rank in the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No rank. I was first a corporal and then a corporal first class. That was my vocation. These are general police ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then later did you join another unit in the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and what unit or -- yeah, what unit was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I became a member of a PJP unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how -- how was you selected for that unit? Did you apply for a position in the unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not apply. I was selected on the basis of my age and my ability. It was our superior who selected the members of the PJP unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was there some sort of a selection process that took place before you were appointed to the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The results of one's physical education, the results of one's work, years of service, all that is taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was there some specific training set up during which you were assessed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no specific training; but later on when we were already members of the PJP, we did have so-called training exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what -- what kind of training exercises were -- were they, the ones in the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Infantry exercises, target practice, attack and defence, jumping out of moving vehicles, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And being a member of the PJP, was that a full-time job or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did normal police work, and we were engaged as needed. This was all within the framework of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what kind of tasks were -- were you carrying out when you were carrying out specific PJP tasks or work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The PJP unit was engaged when there were demonstrations in Belgrade, demonstrations in Pristina, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage, I would ask that we go into private session to deal with some matters that could identify the -- identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, were you sent to Kosovo at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 10th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did your entire detachment go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we should redact the -- the detachment number from the transcript and from the public -- from the transmission of the court hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You think that is necessary, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, without -- how many members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before we -- before we move on, it would help if you did not refer specifically to anything that might identify you. For example, the number of a detachment, which is what happened just now. And your answer's not very clear, because, first of all, you said the entire detachment went, and then you said part of it went and part of the reserve detachment. So which -- which is the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole reserve detachment went and part of the -- well, detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, how -- how many -- how many people were there in your detachment? How big is a detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 150 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Of -- of the entire detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How many members were there in a company, in a PJP company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One hundred fifty, I told you -- oh, no. Sorry, that was a mistake. The detachment had between 500 and 600 members and the company had 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No problem. These sort of things happen. Not to worry. In -- in your company, in addition to the platoons, were there any other units in the company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What were those units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the reconnaissance squad, the command, the mortar squad, the drivers, the cook, the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were -- what was the function of the command section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the command squad, they were in charge of paper, supplying fuel, ammunition, food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It might speak for itself, but the -- the mortar unit or the mortar squad, what -- what did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had two 82-millimetre mortars, and they gave fire support to us when we went into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How many members did the mortar squad have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about ten members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the reconnaissance squad, what size was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around ten members as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How many members of your detachment went to Kosovo approximately, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Our company went then. We went on our own. Whether they were already in Kosovo or whether they came later, I don't know. I mean the members of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there also -- were there some foreigners in -- in your detachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were -- were they -- if you know, were they a separate unit or were they just individual members of different squads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were within a company, but a special separate squad within the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you know when that squad arrived in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When did you -- when did you first hear about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the month of May, when we were handling the village of Budakovo, they were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's just briefly go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, what kind of weapons did you have as a member of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Standard police issue weaponry: An automatic rifle and a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- did you have some additional weapons when you went to -- to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was leaving, no; but when I got to Kosovo, yes, I had hand grenades, rifle grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there some members of your company that had more specialised weapons such as sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Every squad had its own sniper shooter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, what kind of uniforms did you use in the PJP? And let's start with the uniform you used before going to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had working blue camouflage uniforms, and we wore regular police uniforms, the ordinary zone ones. Those in use from 1997. I think, 1997. That's before Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you were in Kosovo, what kind of uniform did you use there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From July 1998 until the 24th of March, 1999, we wore working blue uniforms. From the 24th of March, 1999, we wore NATO uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was the colour of the uniforms you used from July 1998 to March 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blue, bluish grey. Different nuances, different shades of blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In a -- in a camouflage pattern; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and when you had the green uniforms, were they also camouflage uniforms or were they plain colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what were the sort of different colours, if you can describe the colours of the camouflage one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Green, brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on to that, when did you learn that there would be a change in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, before the war, we were issued with these uniforms, NATO uniforms. We were issued these uniforms at the secretariat where I worked; and on the 24th, we were given the order to wear those uniforms, on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long before the 24th were they issued to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, about five months earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you know why you were required to wear different uniforms from -- from the time the war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the uniforms you were given resemble those worn by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you were wearing the blue uniforms, did it -- did it say "Police" on them anywhere or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It said "Milicija" on the blue ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where on the blue ones were that indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the sleeves here; the sleeves of the jackets and the shirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the witness pointed to his shoulder and arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How about on the green uniform? Did it also say "Milicija" on those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you wear anything on top of the green uniforms from time to time, any kind of vest or something to carry equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, combat vests. On the back, it said "Policija."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those vests also worn sometimes together with the blue uniform or only when the green uniform was worn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only when we were in the green uniforms. But from when the war started, we didn't wear any other uniforms except for the green ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you first came to Kosovo, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can you tell us where in Djakovica you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the barracks of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Had you been told why you were going to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Had you been briefed about the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just what I heard on television. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While you were in Djakovica, what kind of duties did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had police patrols. Nothing special, regular police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and how would you describe the situation at that point in time in Djakovica? Was it peaceful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normal situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where did you stay after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we went to Prizren. Again, we were put up at the barracks of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And until when did you stay in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two days. We were in Prizren for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you then leave Prizren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you -- where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you told what you were going to do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were supposed to liberate Orahovac because it had been taken by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you -- were you told this by your commanders, or how did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told in Prizren. No one said anything to us, but we heard these stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember the dates that you were -- left Prizren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 17th or 18th of July. I cannot be sure, but I think it was the 18th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain? How did you leave Prizren? What kind -- did you have some sort of transport? Did you walk? How was that going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trucks and Pinzgauers; that is to say, vehicles that our company had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- how far did you go in the trucks? Until where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First to Bela Crkva and then to the entrance into Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you get off the trucks there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when you arrived at the entrance to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fighting was still going on in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what did your -- what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were waiting in the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you come under fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you approach Orahovac further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We went through all of Orahovac and went to the Serb neighbourhood up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you explain what happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, members of the KLA were withdrawing into the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What -- what units were in Orahovac at that point in time together with you? And here I'm not asking for specific numbers, but -- well, maybe I should put this differently. There was the PJP, obviously. Were there any other police units --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- engaged in the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SAJ, the special Anti-Terrorist Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is that -- is that a police unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you find a suitable place now to interrupt your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why don't we just do it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. For administrative reasons, K79, we do need to have a break now which will be for half an hour. We'll go into closed session to allow you to leave the courtroom with the usher. Just stay where you are for a moment until the blinds come down.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, we were talking about the units that were at Orahovac, and you mentioned the SAJ and explained that they were -- what they were and that they were a police unit. Did you know of this unit before you went to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had heard about them. Everybody had. Among the policemen, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how did you recognise them when you were in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By their uniforms and by the insignia on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The weapons they had, were they the same as yours or were they different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had Hecklers also, at least some individual members of the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you -- would you describe their weapons as having a better quality than yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Apart from the PJP and the SAJ, were there any other armed formations in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except for members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there any military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside of Orahovac, yes, but not in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But did the military, nonetheless, participate in the operation, or were they just outside there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were outside Orahovac, near Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: From what you observed, were they -- were they taking part? Were they having a function in the operation in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they were holding Orahovac in encirclement. There were tanks and Praga, self-propelled anti-aircraft guns, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that -- you mentioned a Praga when you talked about the trucks and vehicles that were moving to Orahovac. Those Pragas, were they belonging to the military or police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the military. The police didn't have any Pragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I don't think that question accurately reflects the evidence. The evidence earlier was that they travelled in trucks and Pinzgauers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. That -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And my question -- yes, sorry. And my question should have been the Pinzgauers, did they belong to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see any captured Albanians while you were in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw one near the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who had captured him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, we would object because it's outside of the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This, in my submission, is relevant to the events that occurred when these sort of operations were carried out. I'm going to explore the fate of this prisoner in my next questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do you say that's covered by the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It fits into -- into the Prosecution's case regarding the nature of the -- these anti-terrorist operations and what was -- how these operations were carried out. We've heard a lot of evidence about how the international community was concerned about excessive use of force, the way these operations were carried out, the effects that these operations had on -- on civilians and people who did not take part in the combat, and it's the Prosecution case that there was a pattern in these operations that started from the very beginning of the operations in March 1998 and carried on right through the entire indictment period. And -- so -- so these events, although they're not charged crimes, we submit is relevant to the assessment of how these so-called anti-terrorist operations were carried out. And, ultimately, all this goes to the issue of whether or not there was a plan. It goes to the knowledge of the accused about the events in -- in Kosovo, and it goes to the knowledge and the continuation of -- these sort of operations go to the issue ultimately of the intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know that in the process of trying to lick this indictment into shape you -- you had the opportunity to select what events in 1998 you would refer to, and I take it from what you've said that this event that you seek to lead evidence about cannot fall within any of the averments in paragraphs 94 and 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I actually left my indictment up in the office, to be frank, but I'm having my assistant -- case manager, of course, is organised and has it. I mean, these -- we do talk about in paragraph -- paragraph 95, the operation that was launched in mid-July 1998 and the destruction and -- and that was caused, so we would submit that that is indeed covered by that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why do you need any specific averments in an indictment at all then? Why don't we just say there was trouble in 1998, 1999, and let's get on with the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think the issue here is -- there's a difference, in our submission, between the individual charged crimes and -- so the individual murders that are charged in the indictment, the individual other specific crimes with which the accused are charged and would be held if found guilty specifically responsible, and then evidence that goes to issues such as intent, existence of a plan, widespread or systematic attack, all these sort of things. There are different requirements with respect to the specificity of these different sort of events, and in one different sort of acts -- so we -- yeah. The fact that -- it shouldn't be impossible for the Prosecution, in my submission, to lead evidence about a specific crime which isn't charged as a specific crime in the indictment as long as it goes to another issue that's relevant in the case. Now, we're not -- and we've said this before, we're not going to submit that the accused are responsible for the killings that occurred in 1998 or other crimes that occurred, but the fact that these different -- that a number of different crimes were committed in 1998 is relevant to the issues, kind of issues I've already outlined. So on that basis, we submit that this evidence is admissible. And, again, the statement has been -- we sought to have this witness added to the witness list before the trial started. The statement has been disclosed for a long time. It has been clear to the Defence that we were going to lead this evidence. I submit there cannot be any prejudice to the accused from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, the difficulty I have is understanding what an indictment is for in this case. What is the purpose of the indictment if you just lead whatever evidence you've intimated in statements? What is the indictment is supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The indictment is supposed to put the Defence of notice of the allegations that are being leveled against specificity. There are different degrees of specificity that we have to set different facts out, for we do not, in our submission, need to set out every single individual crime and specify every single incident in a long chronology of events in the indictment. We need to give a description that informs the Defence about the nature of the Prosecution's case. We've done that. Further particulars has been provided in the pre-trial brief, and we're going to lead evidence and that's the last step in the process, and the Defence has to right to know what the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this incidence is in the pre-trial brief is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The campaign in July is mentioned in the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it's also mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it then goes on to say which elements of that campaign are being relied upon in the case. And it's a very wide-ranging area of Kosovo that's covered, but it doesn't seem to relate to events in Orahovac. Now, why is that? Why have you not referred to all these other places and not made this reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This particular indictment -- I mean, it's a timing issue. The witness wasn't on the witness list at the time that the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But an indictment can be amended at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Right. I think in -- in June when -- it was a fairly long process to get this indictment in place. The Prosecution was trying to show some restraint in continuing to amend the indictment in order to -- not to block the commencement of the trial. We tried to -- to do some -- make some choices there, and we have had evidence about a number of incidents which are not charged. We could have charged some -- a lot of this -- many things as individual crimes. The choice was not to do that and to accept that some of this evidence can only be used for other purposes, and we're not ultimately going to be able to allege the accused are responsible for this. Now, that is the rationale for the course of conduct that we've had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you intending to say something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I did want to maybe refer Your Honours to paragraph 27 of the pre-trial brief, where there's talk about the KLA conducting operations in various areas, including Orahovac; and then it mentions that the forces of the FRY and Serbia responded, that there was a campaign of shelling and persecution. But it's in the pre-trial brief. It's not in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's a reference to 1998, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you indicated you wanted to say something else also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After these new informations I got from my learned friend, we find it appropriate only if they think that this Albanian is killed by shells, and obviously it's not the case. And you, Your Honour, put us on notice that we should object every time when we find it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not at all critical of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And still we think it's not pled in the indictment specifically, and specifically not -- not in the pre-trial brief as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We -- we don't want to discourage objection. I know that in the past when we've made a ruling adverse to the Defence, there has been hesitancy sometimes in -- on the part of Defence counsel in continuing to object. So I make it clear that we don't by this decision mean to discourage that, because we need guidance on this point. It does seem to us that there's potential relevance in this evidence, bearing in mind that it's said that the activity of this group continues through into 1999. And bearing in mind some of the other more general considerations mentioned by Mr. Marcussen, we find it very difficult to judge this objection knowing of that potential, and, therefore, we will reserve a final decision on it and allow this evidence to be led. There may come a time even during the evidence when we can take a final decision, but perhaps not. Perhaps that final decision will have to wait a later stage in the trial. If we can make it final, we will do so in the course of the witness's evidence. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, so we -- you said that members of the SAJ had captured an Albanian civilian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think this is a misrepresentation of the evidence. Here we have an Albanian civilian, and I think the witness said something else. I'm not sure, but I think that -- he said KLA, and he didn't say who captured him, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think these -- I just cover these things. I break it down. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I think you should start this episode again and make sure that your questions are open questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, did you see any captured persons while you were in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had been captured. I know he was there surrounded by members of the SAJ. He was saying, "It wasn't me. It wasn't me." That's all I know. Whether he had been captured or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe the clothes this person was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he had white trousers and a white shirt on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did he have any weapons as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, no, he didn't. I don't know whether he had had before that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember what age, approximately, he looked like he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say. Young-ish, not more than 40, but I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At the time was it your impression that he was a fighter of some sort, a soldier or member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This really calls for speculation. He described the man. This only can help us, of course, but it calls for speculation, and that's why we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that question is okay, because it will need to be followed up depending on what the answer is, and we need a starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, at the time did you -- did you form an opinion about whether this person was a fighter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a fighter. I do know that many members of the KLA wore civilian clothes but carried weapons. Now, whether this was the case with this man, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What happened to the man after he had said, "It was not me," as you just explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A member of the SAJ shot him dead with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How far away from -- from these events were you when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So could you see the man who -- who shot this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and you heard? You were close enough to hear what this person said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What person do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The person who got shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before he was shot, all I understand him to say was, "It wasn't me. It wasn't me."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and -- but you heard him say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and how do you know that it was a member of the SAJ who shot this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 30 members of the SAJ in that area, in that place. I knew them by their uniforms and their insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you see the insignia on the person who fired the gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had badges saying "SAJ" on their shoulders. I mean, not a badge but an insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and the man -- did you also see the insignia on the man who fired the gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on him, but he had the same uniform as all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. After this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very confusing now. Are you saying that there was something missing from his uniform, or are you saying you didn't see whether or not he had "SAJ" on the shoulder? What is the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not notice it on his uniform. I noticed it on some other members who were around him. Some had insignia on, some didn't. Some were in T-shirts, others wore jackets. The ones who had jackets on had insignia, and the ones who were wearing T-shirts didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened next? How long did you stay at this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent about 30 minutes in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The members of the KLA were on the surrounding hills near Orahovac. We could hear shooting from up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe how these members of the KLA were looking? Were they wearing uniforms? Were they wearing weapons? How did they look?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them wore uniforms; some wore civilian clothes; and some had our blue work uniforms, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did they carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They had automatic rifles. They also had Brownings set up on the hills overlooking Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so the people in civilian, were they also carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain us what a Browning is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a 12.7-millimetre machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So you stayed in this place for about half an hour, then what -- where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we passed through Orahovac and went to the Serbian part of Orahovac, closer to the hills from which they were shooting at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In trucks, Pinzgauers, and jeeps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what you saw as you were driving on the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout Orahovac I saw about 30 corpses along the road, approximately. I cannot say for sure what the number was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were they lying in one location or in different places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in one location; that is to say, throughout town, one would be here, another one would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The corpses you saw, were they -- were you able to see whether they were men or women or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part it was men; only one woman at the exit towards Malisevo. All of them were younger men up to the age of 40, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember whether any of the dead bodies were wearing any kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that two wore uniforms, camouflage uniforms. The German uniforms. I don't know. The others were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see whether there were any weapons lying by the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Actually, maybe my question was not entirely clear. Did you see any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In town, no. In the hills, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where did the trucks take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the exit from Orahovac towards Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the trucks stop there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were shooting at us from the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you remain in the truck or did you get off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then could you explain what happened there? You got off and then what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we started walking towards the hill from where they were shooting at us. In about an hour, we took the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vran-stena.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How -- how long did you stay at the hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what happened during those three days, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were guarding the hill and there was sporadic gunfire. That's it. Nothing important happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When those three days over, were you replaced by someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. A replacement came after three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And without giving any specific numbers, who -- of any units or anything, who --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- who replaced you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A unit from our detachment, a reserve unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where did you go when you were replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went down to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you -- did you stay at Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Until the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there any continued fighting while you were in Orahovac, so before September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you sent out on operations, then, in the month of September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We were in action throughout the month of September. We practically covered the entire territory of Kosovo during that month or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How long would each of these operations last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from five to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And between the operations, would you go back to Orahovac, or where would you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We would return. That's where our base was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you remember, the name of any of the places that you were going for operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I think that the last time when I objected, my learned explained that there is mentioning of July in their submissions, the indictment, and pre-trial brief. Now we are discussing September and onwards. So I think that there is nothing regarding these operations. If that can be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the middle of paragraph 95, we talk about first operations in mid-July, then August, and then September. So the arguments are the same as I've set out before. There would be some specific locations mentioned which are in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief; but as is obvious from the evidence, this witness participated in a -- in a series of operations throughout the month in different locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you going to be leading evidence in relation to places that are covered by the references to events in August and September in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them -- I mean, the thing is some of these descriptions in the indictment and pre-trial brief are broad, and there's a question about what the definition of what a specific area is. Some of the specific locations are mentioned. Some of it is in more general areas, but I would say we are on fairly safe ground here. But I don't know if my colleague objects to that description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me the paragraph in the pre-trial brief. Did you say it was 27?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Twenty-seven, yes. My apologies. And we also should refer to paragraph 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. In paragraph 92, it's Drenica area that's mentioned, and that does not include places mentioned by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, there are mentioned places like Glogovac, and a number of those locations are mentioned by the witness, I believe. There are also locations that are mentioned that are not, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In any event, your position, Mr. Marcussen, is that the indictment actually relates to areas which you say you're now going to lead evidence about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the witness is going to talk about places that have been described as hamlets in different areas, so it's very difficult for me to pin down precisely where some of these locations are. They are in these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if we find that these areas that are referred to do not fall within the terms of the indictment and possibly the pre-trial brief, then we'll review the position again and we'll expect Mr. Lukic to draw our attention to that if that's what happens. Meanwhile, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So, K79, so you said that during the month of September went to various areas in Kosovo. On operations, you would go back to Orahovac, which was your base. Now, would -- could you please -- my question was if you could mention the places in which operations took place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. We're having -- the interpreter is having difficulty. If you could come slightly closer to the microphone and start your answer again, please. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were carrying out actions in Drenica, at Bajgora, at Cicavica, and other places, and I don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cleaning up the terrain from members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how was that done? How do you carry out an operation like that? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my unit has an axis of activity and then we are cleaning up KLA strongholds in front of us, villages where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you say "cleaning up," you ensure that there are no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by -- could you explain what you mean by "cleaning up"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean expelling members of the KLA from that terrain or neutralising them. It's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you -- could you describe the steps in an operation like that? You go out to a certain location and then what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You go to a location where members of the KLA are, either a hill or a village; and if they are well-fortified, then the mortars come into action, and then we go and clean the village from members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Does that entail checking various locations for whether or not there are any KLA members there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sent to locations where there were members of the KLA; that is to say, when we would get to such a location, they would shoot at us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like my learned friend to specify with the witness a period of time when these operations took place. Because if it's in the indictment or in the pre-trial brief that something happened in 1999, we think that if this witness is talking about 1998, it's not covered by the indictment and by the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at the moment we're in September 1998, as I understand the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the indictment and the pre-trial brief, we do have Bajgora, Drenica, Cicavica; but in 1999, not in 1998. That's what I could find in this heap at the moment. I apologise. There is Bajgora mentioned in 1998, in paragraph 27 in the pre-trial brief, not in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, your ongoing objection is noted, and we'll continue to listen to this and see what it amounts to in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, when -- when -- when a KLA position, let's say within a village, had been taken over by you, you had overcome the opposing force, what would your next step be? Was there a next step in the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We'd go on. We would not stay in that village. We would follow the enemy further on, or we would go to other villages where there were members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would -- would various houses in a village be checked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was anything else done to the houses? Was there anything done to the houses apart from checking them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have three exhibits that I'd like to show to the witness. Now, this might identify the witness, so I don't know whether we need to go into private session or whether we can show the exhibits without broadcasting the image outside the courtroom. I'm seeking guidance on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They can usually be shown without broadcast. Is that -- that's how it will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we call up Exhibit P2624.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, K79, a picture will be shown on the monitor in front of you. K79, the picture that we see here, are you familiar with that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Without mentioning the name, do you know who took the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know where this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing to object to. Yes, I note the position. But unless there's some substance put on this, then it's a pointless exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, to your knowledge, is this picture taken in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I don't know the exact location. It can be Drenica. It can be Cicavica. I don't know the exact location where this was taken. It was taken in Kosovo though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know about what time it was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you know these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the man who took this picture talked to me about it. I mean, he was there with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, where did he speak to you? I'm not following this. You said you did not know where it was taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact location, but I saw these pictures earlier on, too. These pictures were taken in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe it would clarify matters if we went into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how do you know this picture was taken in September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was there with him when he took the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we would expect you to know where it was then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can -- I cannot remember exactly where it was. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, is -- is this how things looked during the operations you were carrying out? Is this a correct sort of image of how things were looking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, to me it looks like there's some smoke coming up from a location. Do you know -- is that right? Is it smoke that we have in the middle of the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where's that smoke coming from? You don't know the location, but where does the smoke come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The smoke is coming from houses that are burning and haystacks that are burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like now if we could call -- could we see Exhibit P2626. 2626.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, what about this picture? Do you know where this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it's the same location like the previous one, but I don't know where it is exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In -- a little to the left of the house, there seems to be some sort of a vehicle. What is that, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: During your operations, did you have tanks with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had tanks and Pragas attached to our unit. One or two tanks and two or three Pragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did those tanks belong to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, to the army. The MUP doesn't have tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: During the operations, who would give orders to the tanks and the Pragas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would now actually like to move on now to Exhibit P2625. If we could call that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you even remember the circumstances that occurred in this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was most probably a KLA stronghold because it was set on fire. Those villages where there were KLA strongholds were set on fire. Where there was no KLA, the house were is not torched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why were the houses torched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there people in them when they were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you involved in setting them on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who did it then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was done by individuals and detachments from Kosovo; detachments of the PJP from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that none of your detachment did any of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some individuals from my detachment did, two or three perhaps, following orders from the company commander. Nobody else participated in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Were you aware of your company commander ordering this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The company commander, yes. I heard him order a man to set fire to a house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Could we call up Exhibit P2625.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, again, is this a photograph from the same period in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you there when this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But -- well, do you remember where it was? I guess I have to put the question that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the precise location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it different from the other two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think it's the same village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's burning here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume the inside of the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you were there. Can you remember what it was that was actually burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would usually set fire to the curtains and to the wall panelling. Albanian houses usually had panelling inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But it was the house that was burning. Is that the correct understanding of your answer, the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You were there when the picture was taken. Do you -- do you happen to know who set this particular house on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was it a member of your detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we should go just briefly into private session to get the identity of the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, these operations in September, who ordered the operations, as far as you know? And no names but just positions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before every action, our company commander would come to see us in the morning and give us the plan of the action. He would tell us where to go and what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And do you know where your company commander had received his instructions from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume the detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: "Assume." Why do you say "assume"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be sure who he got them from, but it would be logical for him to get them from the detachment commander. I only heard our company commander issuing orders. They had briefings. They had meetings. And I assume that the commander, the detachment commander, issued orders as to what we were to do and where we were to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. And your detachment -- detachment commander, where did he get his orders from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any meetings taking place in Pristina before any of your operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Pristina? Not in Pristina. It was in Prizren that the company commanders had meetings with the detachment commander. I don't know about Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know whether your detachment commander had meetings with any of the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know whether your detachment commander had any meetings with a gentleman called Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have heard that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already had that question answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think I would like to, with the Court's permission, put a part of the witness statement to him and ask him about a specific part of that statement at this point in time. Now, this is done in different ways in different cases, but I think I would like to try to refresh the witness's memory on one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If my learned friend is impeaching his own witness, we would understand that; but, otherwise, he had his question answered two times, and we would object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I see the statement, please, and the paragraph that's relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's paragraph 17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what's the significance you attach to the suggestion that he may be -- that Mr. Marcussen may be impeaching his own witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you read that part of the statement and, obviously, we have a different answer now, although it's not clear whether that part of statement is in any connection with any action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't have any -- any different answer though. All I'm doing is looking at this to see what -- what's the appropriate step to take in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In -- on page 48, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a question: "Do you know whether your detachment commander had any meetings with any of the accused," and he said "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. That could mean that he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm trying to understand is your reference to impeachment. What you're saying is that he can challenge the witness? Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's our point, and I think that he is challenging his witness. He got an answer -- two answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and he may do that. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that he cannot, otherwise he can -- he only can say that he does not want this witness and does not want his testimony today here if he's impeaching his own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what's your authority for that proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can't recall by heart from the previous trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. You say that's a rule of this Tribunal, do you? It's not one I'm familiar with, but I'm here to be educated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that something similar happened in Omarska 1 case. We had discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, I'm familiar with a process being followed here in at least one other case where a witness was declared hostile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then he has to declare him being hostile and to establish why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find it difficult to see what the significance of all that is just from a common sense point of view. I just don't understand, at the moment, why it's necessary to go through some formal process when what may be involved is simply a jogging of the memory. It's not clear to me at the moment that what would happen would be more than simply jogging the witnesses memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They had the chance to jog his memory, and we think that that question was asked and answered two times. Now we have -- my learn friend is trying to ask the witness the same question a third time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not satisfied that it's entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, therefore, I'm going to ask a question myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if you can establish the time frame, please, and in relation with what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: May I address a legal point before that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I asked the Chamber what guidance on the procedure here, because there have been instances where the hostile witness approach has been taken. I also don't remember my precise case for this, but there is at least one instance where this kind of procedure has not been adopted in this place. I think in many places you can refresh a witness memory. We can also -- I can keep this question and we can do the legal research and come back to you on this, if that assists Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K79, the Prosecutor is anxious to know whether you have any knowledge of any meeting between your detachment commander and any of the accused, and that includes whether you had ever heard of such meetings. He's not confining his question to simply the situation where you personally were aware of it. Now, what is the position? Have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear about such meetings. Your Honour, my commander had meetings with Obrad Stefanovic, the commander of the PJP units. Mr. Lukic was not the commander of the PJP units, and I don't see why they would have to meet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's the number, Mr. Marcussen, of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, it -- the statement doesn't -- it isn't yet uploaded into the system because he was, as was discussed this morning, initially thought of as a live witness. We could add the statement, and it would then have Exhibit number P2653.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In May of last year, May 2006, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in that statement, it says that your detachment commander, whom you name in the statement, used to go to meetings with Sreten Lukic in Pristina; and you say that you knew this because your deputy company commander, and you name him, told you about these meetings; and you also say that on one occasion you drove to one of these meetings in Prizren. Now -- sorry. Ignore the last part of the driving's to a different meeting.
